subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are angles in a triangle, then prove that sin²A + sin²B − sin²C = 2 sin A sin B cos C.

mark_split.label: Replace sin A inside the bracket

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.107 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 167. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's own inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: classed LAQ on its length and shape — a transformation identity on a triangle, the exact shape of Unit 6's own LAQ chapter. The bank prints no mark cut, so this classification is OURS. Printed appearances: AP 19. The condition A + B + C = 180° is used TWICE — once to turn sin(B+C) into sin A, and once to turn sin A back into sin(B+C). Those are not the same move, and both are needed. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular split for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Replace B + C by 180° − A.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Group the last two terms
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks. Bracket sin²B − sin²C — the two that differ in sign — and apply sin²A − sin²B = sin(A+B) sin(A−B).

recall.must_convey: That sin²B − sin²C is grouped and turned into sin(B+C) sin(B−C).
accept: group the last two terms and use sin squared B minus sin squared C equals sin of B plus C into sin of B minus C
bracket the two terms that differ in sign
apply the difference of squares to the last pair
chivari rendu group chesi difference of squares apply cheyyali
group and use the identity

steps.why: The minus sign sits between the second and third terms, so those two are the pair. Grouping the first two instead gives a sum, not a difference.
common_mistakes: Using cos²B − cos²C, which carries an extra minus.

steps.label: Replace B + C by 180° − A
steps.margin_note: Two marks (third and fourth). From A + B + C = 180°, B + C = 180° − A, and sin(180° − A) = sin A.
lines: ⇒ sin(B + C) = sin(180° − A) = sin A
L.H.S = sin²A + sin A sin(B − C)

recall.must_convey: That B + C = 180° − A gives sin(B+C) = sin A.
accept: B plus C is one eighty minus A and sine of one eighty minus A is sine A
use the angle sum to replace sin of B plus C by sin A
sin of one eighty minus A equals sin A
B plus C ante one eighty minus A, sin same
apply the triangle angle sum

steps.why: sin(180° − A) = sin A but cos(180° − A) = −cos A. Only the sine is unchanged by the shift, which is why this route uses sines.

steps.label: Take sin A common
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Both terms now carry sin A, so factor it out — everything that follows happens inside the bracket.
lines: L.H.S = sin A [sin A + sin(B − C)]

recall.must_convey: That sin A is taken out as a common factor, leaving sin A + sin(B − C) inside.
accept: both terms have sin A so take it outside leaving sin A plus sin of B minus C
factor out sin A
take the common factor out
rendu terms lo sin A undi, bayata teeyali
pull sin A out as a common factor

steps.why: The right-hand side has 2 sin A sin B cos C — one sin A outside is exactly what is wanted, and the rest of the work is on the bracket.

steps.label: Replace sin A inside the bracket
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Inside the bracket, write sin A back as sin(B+C) — the reverse of step 2, so both terms become sines of B and C.
lines: Inside the bracket, sin A = sin(180° − (B + C))

recall.must_convey: That sin A inside the bracket is written as sin(B + C), so the bracket is sin(B+C) + sin(B−C).
accept: write sin A inside the bracket as sin of B plus C so both terms involve B and C
reverse the earlier substitution inside the bracket only
the bracket becomes sin B plus C plus sin B minus C
bracket lo sin A ni sin B plus C ga marchali
substitute back inside the bracket

steps.why: The sin A outside is kept and the sin A inside is converted — the same quantity treated two different ways, because the bracket needs a sum-to-product shape.
common_mistakes: Leaving the bracket as sin A + sin(B − C) and trying to close from there.

steps.label: Apply the sum formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. sin(X+Y) + sin(X−Y) = 2 sin X cos Y with X = B, Y = C gives 2 sin B cos C.
lines: sin(B + C) + sin(B − C) = 2 sin B cos C
L.H.S = sin A · 2 sin B cos C

lines.text: ∴ sin²A + sin²B − sin²C = 2 sin A sin B cos C

recall.must_convey: That sin(B+C) + sin(B−C) = 2 sin B cos C, closing the proof.
accept: sin of B plus C plus sin of B minus C is two sin B cos C which closes the proof
the bracket becomes two sin B cos C
multiply by the sin A outside to reach the right hand side
bracket two sin B cos C, sin A tho multiply cheste answer
apply the sum to product formula

steps.why: The pair sin(X+Y) + sin(X−Y) always collapses to 2 sin X cos Y. It is the same identity used in step 1, run in the other direction.
common_mistakes: Writing 2 cos B sin C instead.
Stopping before multiplying by the outside sin A.
